title: Modern Indian History
summary: From Vasco da Gama to 1947: British expansion and the Governor-Generals, the Revolt of 1857, reform movements, early Congress, the Gandhian movements, revolutionaries, and the newspapers and books of the freedom struggle. It is the most-asked history block in SSC CGL. Expect 1–2 questions per shift, mostly event–year, reform–Governor-General and founder–organisation pairs.

tricks.title: Plassey then Buxar — "57 buys, 64 seals"
tricks.body: **1757 Plassey** gave the British a foothold (Clive vs Siraj); **1764 Buxar** sealed control (three Indian rulers beaten) and brought the **Diwani (1765)**.

example.q: Which battle was fought against the combined forces of Mir Qasim, Shuja-ud-Daula and Shah Alam II?
example.solution: Three rulers together → **Buxar (1764)**.

tricks.title: Governor-General reforms — "Cornwallis Settles, Wellesley Subsidises, Bentinck bans Sati, Ripon Rules locally"

mistakes: Warren Hastings = first GG of **Bengal**; William Bentinck = first GG of **India**; Canning = first **Viceroy**.
Ilbert Bill is **Ripon's** era, not Curzon's.
The English first factory was at **Surat**; Calicut is linked with Vasco da Gama.
subtopics.notes:
### From traders to rulers
The East India Company got its charter in **1600** and its first factory at **Surat** (1612, after the naval win over the Portuguese). It then built three presidencies: **Madras (1639)**, **Bombay (1668, from Charles II's dowry)** and **Calcutta (1690, Job Charnock)**. After beating the French (Dupleix) in the **Carnatic wars**, the Company turned on Bengal: at **Plassey (1757)** Robert Clive defeated **Siraj-ud-Daulah** through **Mir Jafar's** betrayal; at **Buxar (1764)** it defeated the combined armies of **Mir Qasim, Shuja-ud-Daula and Emperor Shah Alam II**. The **Treaty of Allahabad (1765)** gave the Company the **Diwani** (revenue rights) of Bengal-Bihar-Odisha; Clive's 'dual government' (1765–72) was ended by **Warren Hastings**, the first Governor-General under the **Regulating Act 1773** (Pitt's India Act 1784 added dual control).

### Wars that made the empire
- **Mysore:** four wars against Haidar Ali and **Tipu Sultan**; Tipu — the 'Tiger of Mysore' — died defending **Srirangapatna in 1799** (Fourth war, Wellesley).
- **Marathas:** three Anglo-Maratha wars ended Maratha power (**1818**).
- **Sikhs:** two wars after Ranjit Singh's death (1839) — Punjab **annexed 1849** (Dalhousie).
- **Others:** Sind (1843, Napier), Burma, Awadh annexed 1856 'for misgovernment'.
- **Subsidiary Alliance** (Wellesley, Nizam first in 1798): the ally kept Company troops and lost independence; **Doctrine of Lapse** (Dalhousie): adopted heirs refused — **Satara, Jaitpur, Sambalpur, Udaipur, Jhansi, Nagpur** lapsed.

### Governor-Generals' landmarks
**Cornwallis** (1786–93): **Permanent Settlement (1793)**, police and judicial reforms, 'father of the Indian civil service'. **William Bentinck** (1828–35): **sati abolished (1829)**, English education (Macaulay's Minute 1835), thuggee suppressed. **Dalhousie** (1848–56): railways (1853), telegraph, postage, engineering colleges — the infrastructure age plus annexations. **Lytton**: **Vernacular Press Act (1878)**, Arms Act, and the Delhi Durbar of 1877 proclaiming Victoria 'Empress of India'.

### The three land-revenue systems
| System | Region | Key feature |
|---|---|---|
| **Permanent Settlement (1793)** | Bengal-Bihar-Odisha | Zamindars fixed as landowners; revenue fixed forever (Cornwallis) |
| **Ryotwari** | Madras, Bombay | Settlement directly with the **ryot** (cultivator); Reed & **Thomas Munro** |
| **Mahalwari** | North-Western Provinces, Central India, parts of Punjab | Settlement with the **village estate (mahal)**; Holt Mackenzie, 1822 |

### Quick revision
- Plassey 1757 (Mir Jafar) → Buxar 1764 (triple alliance beaten) → Diwani 1765 (Treaty of Allahabad).
- Tipu died 1799 at Srirangapatna; Marathas ended 1818; Punjab 1849.
- Wellesley = Subsidiary Alliance; Dalhousie = Doctrine of Lapse + railways; Lytton = Vernacular Press Act 1878.
- Revenue trio: Permanent (Cornwallis, zamindari), Ryotwari (Munro, ryot), Mahalwari (Holt Mackenzie, village).

patterns.name: Company victories: Plassey → Buxar → Diwani chain
patterns.howToSpot: 'Who was defeated at Buxar', what the Treaty of Allahabad granted, Mir Jafar's role, order of events 1757-1765.
patterns.logic:
1. **Plassey 1757** = Clive vs Siraj-ud-Daulah (Mir Jafar betrayed); **Buxar 1764** = vs Mir Qasim + Shuja-ud-Daula + Shah Alam II.
2. **Treaty of Allahabad 1765** = **Diwani of Bengal, Bihar, Odisha** to the Company.
3. Diwani means revenue-collection rights — not territory ownership.

example.solution: **Emperor Shah Alam II** — after which the Treaty of Allahabad granted the Company the Diwani.

patterns.name: Governor-General ↔ policy and landmark measure

patterns.name: Land-revenue systems: zamindari, ryotwari, mahalwari
patterns.howToSpot: 'The Ryotwari system was introduced by', which region had Mahalwari, Permanent Settlement features.
patterns.logic:
1. **Permanent Settlement 1793 (Cornwallis)** — Bengal-Bihar-Odisha, zamindari, revenue fixed.
2. **Ryotwari (Reed & Thomas Munro)** — Madras and Bombay; settlement with each cultivator.
3. **Mahalwari (Holt Mackenzie, 1822)** — NW Provinces, Central India, parts of Punjab; village estate (mahal).

example.q: The **Ryotwari** system, settling revenue directly with each cultivator, was developed mainly in —
example.solution: **Madras and Bombay** presidencies, associated with Reed and **Thomas Munro**.

subtopics.title: Revolt of 1857 and Peasant & Tribal Uprisings
subtopics.concept:
**Revolt of 1857**

| Point | Fact |
|---|---|
| Immediate cause | **Enfield rifle** cartridges said to be greased with cow and pig fat |

tricks.title: 1857 pairs — "Kanpur Nana, Lucknow Lady, Jhansi Rani, Bihar Kunwar"
tricks.body: **K**anpur–**N**ana Saheb · **L**ucknow–Begum Hazrat Mahal (the Lady) · **J**hansi–Rani Lakshmibai · **B**ihar (Jagdishpur)–Kunwar Singh, the 80-year-old.

example.q: Kunwar Singh led the revolt of 1857 in which region?
example.solution: **Jagdishpur, Bihar**.

mistakes: The revolt **broke out at Meerut** (10 May); Barrackpore saw Mangal Pandey's earlier act.
Rani Lakshmibai was defeated by **Hugh Rose**, not Colin Campbell.
Bahadur Shah Zafar was exiled to **Rangoon**, not the Andamans.
subtopics.notes:
### The spark and the tinder
On **29 March 1857** at **Barrackpore**, **Mangal Pandey** of the **34th Native Infantry** attacked his officers over the **greased cartridges** of the new Enfield rifle (rumoured greased with cow and pig fat) — he was hanged on 8 April. On **10 May 1857** the sepoys at **Meerut** (85 troopers of the 3rd Light Cavalry, dismissed for refusing cartridges, were jailed) broke out, marched to Delhi and proclaimed the old **Bahadur Shah II** 'Emperor of India'. The greased cartridge was only the **immediate cause**.

### Deeper causes
- **Political:** Doctrine of Lapse annexations (Satara, Jhansi, Nagpur), Awadh annexed (1856), disrespect to the Mughal house, Nana Saheb's pension denied.
- **Economic:** heavy land revenue, ruin of handicrafts (de-industrialisation), drain of wealth, loss of zamindari and talukdari rights.
- **Social-religious:** reform laws (sati abolition), the Religious Disabilities Act (1850, converts could inherit), rumours about railways-telegraphs, missionary activity.
- **Military:** sepoys' pay and promotion grievances, the **General Service Enlistment Act (1856)** (service across the sea, feared caste-loss), Indians barred from officer ranks.

### Centres and leaders
| Centre | Leader |
|---|---|
| Delhi | Bahadur Shah II (general **Bakht Khan**) |
| **Kanpur** | **Nana Saheb** (with **Tantia Tope**, Azimullah Khan) |
| **Lucknow** | **Begum Hazrat Mahal** |
| **Jhansi** | **Rani Lakshmibai** |
| **Arrah/Jagdishpur (Bihar)** | **Kunwar Singh** |
| Faizabad | **Maulvi Ahmadullah Shah** |
| **Bareilly** | **Khan Bahadur Khan** |

The revolt spread through the Ganga plain, central India and parts of the Deccan; Bombay, Madras, Punjab (mostly) and Bengal proper stayed quiet — so it is called a 'sepoy mutiny' by some historians and the 'First War of Independence' (V.D. Savarkar's phrase) by others.

### Suppression and aftermath
Delhi fell in **September 1857**; the Emperor was tried and exiled to **Rangoon**. Jhansi's Rani died fighting at **Gwalior (June 1858)**; Tantia Tope was captured and hanged (1859). The **Government of India Act, 1858** ended Company rule — a **Secretary of State for India** took charge, the Governor-General became **Viceroy** (**Canning** first), and **Queen Victoria's Proclamation** (Allahabad, 1 November 1858) promised no more annexations and religious non-interference. The army was reconstituted along 'divide and rule' lines.

### Peasant and tribal uprisings
- **Paika rebellion, 1817** (Odisha) — **Bakshi Jagabandhu** against the British land system.
- **Kol uprising, 1831** (Chotanagpur) — tribal lands taken by outsiders.
- **Santhal Hul, 1855-56** — **Sidhu and Kanhu** Murmu against moneylenders and colonial revenue.
- **Munda Ulgulan, 1899-1900** — **Birsa Munda**; led to the Chotanagpur Tenancy Act (1908).
- **Faraizi movement** (Bengal, Dudu Mian); **Moplah uprisings** (Malabar, peaks in 1921).

### Quick revision
- Immediate cause: greased cartridges; spark: Barrackpore (Mangal Pandey, 34th NI); outbreak: Meerut, 10 May 1857.
- Centre-leader pairs: Kanpur-Nana Saheb, Lucknow-Hazrat Mahal, Jhansi-Lakshmibai, Arrah-Kunwar Singh, Bareilly-Khan Bahadur Khan, Faizabad-Ahmadullah Shah.
- Aftermath: Act of 1858 ends Company rule; Viceroy Canning; Queen's Proclamation, Allahabad, 1 Nov 1858.
- Uprisings: Paika 1817 (Jagabandhu), Santhal 1855 (Sidhu-Kanhu), Munda 1899 (Birsa).

patterns.howToSpot: 'Who led the revolt at X', match-the-column of centres and leaders, 'Kunwar Singh fought at'.
patterns.logic:
1. The table: Delhi-Bahadur Shah II, Kanpur-Nana Saheb, Lucknow-Hazrat Mahal, Jhansi-Lakshmibai, Arrah-Kunwar Singh, Faizabad-Ahmadullah Shah, Bareilly-Khan Bahadur Khan.
2. Assistant leaders: Tantia Tope (Kanpur campaign), Bakht Khan (Delhi).

example.solution: **Kunwar Singh**, the 80-year-old zamindar of Jagdishpur.

patterns.name: Causes: immediate trigger and deeper discontent
patterns.howToSpot: 'Immediate cause of 1857', greased cartridges, General Service Enlistment Act, annexation causes, 'which was NOT a cause'.
patterns.logic:
1. **Immediate**: Enfield greased cartridges (cow-pig rumour) → Mangal Pandey, Barrackpore, 34th NI.
2. Deeper: Lapse annexations, Awadh 1856, revenue burden, de-industrialisation, 1856 Enlistment Act, reform laws.
3. In 'NOT a cause' questions, look for something post-1857 (e.g. Partition of Bengal) — that's the odd one.

example.q: The **General Service Enlistment Act (1856)** worried sepoys because it —
example.solution: Required service **across the sea**, which many believed would cost them caste.

patterns.name: Course, suppression and the 1858 Act
patterns.howToSpot: 'Revolt began at Meerut on', Bahadur Shah's fate, Government of India Act 1858 provisions, Queen's Proclamation.
patterns.logic:
1. Chain: Barrackpore (29 March) → Meerut (10 May 1857) → Delhi proclaimed; Delhi falls September 1857.
2. **Bahadur Shah II** — tried and exiled to **Rangoon**; sons shot by Hodson.
3. **Act of 1858**: Company ends, Secretary of State, **Viceroy = Canning**; Queen's Proclamation (Allahabad, 1 Nov 1858) promises no annexation, no religious interference.

example.q: The **Government of India Act, 1858** did which of the following?
example.solution: Ended East India Company rule; India came under the Crown, with a Secretary of State and the Viceroy (Canning) at the head.

patterns.name: Peasant and tribal uprisings ↔ leaders
patterns.howToSpot: 'Santhal rebellion was led by', Birsa Munda's movement, Paika rebellion, Faraizi/Moplah facts.
patterns.logic:
1. **Paika 1817 — Bakshi Jagabandhu** (Odisha); **Kol 1831** (Chotanagpur); **Santhal Hul 1855 — Sidhu & Kanhu**.
2. **Munda Ulgulan 1899-1900 — Birsa Munda** (later honoured as 'Dharti Aba'); Chotanagpur Tenancy Act 1908 followed.
3. Faraizi = Bengal (Dudu Mian); Moplah = Malabar (peaks 1921).

example.q: The **Santhal rebellion (1855-56)**, called the Hul, was led by —
example.solution: **Sidhu and Kanhu** Murmu — against moneylenders and colonial revenue men.

tricks.title: 1875 — the year of three
tricks.body: **Arya Samaj** (Dayanand), **Theosophical Society** (Blavatsky–Olcott) and the **Aligarh MAO school** (Syed Ahmad Khan) all date to **1875**.

example.q: Which two of these began in the same year — Arya Samaj, Brahmo Samaj, Theosophical Society, Ramakrishna Mission?
example.solution: **Arya Samaj and Theosophical Society** (both 1875).

tricks.title: Founder hooks
tricks.body: **R**am Mohan = **R**eform of sati (Brahmo, 1828) · **D**ayanand = **D**iscover the Vedas (Arya) · **P**hule = **P**eople of lower castes (Satyashodhak) · **V**ivekananda = **V**edanta service (RK Mission, 1897).

mistakes: Ramakrishna Mission was founded by **Vivekananda** (1897), not Ramakrishna Paramahamsa himself.
Theosophical Society was founded in **New York**, then moved to Adyar.
Widow Remarriage Act 1856 = **Vidyasagar**; sati abolition 1829 = Ram Mohan Roy's campaign.
subtopics.notes:
### Awakening the 19th century
**Raja Ram Mohan Roy** — the 'father of modern India' — began with the Atmiya Sabha (1814) and founded the **Brahmo Sabha/Samaj (1828)**, preaching monotheism and against idolatry. He campaigned against **sati** (abolished **1829** under Bentinck, with his persuasion), for widow remarriage, a free press and English education; his works include the *Gift to Monotheists*. **Debendranath Tagore** (Tattvabodhini Sabha) and **Keshab Chandra Sen** later led the Brahmo Samaj through its splits.
**Ishwar Chandra Vidyasagar** carried the widow-remarriage campaign to law — the **Hindu Widows' Remarriage Act, 1856** — and wrote the Bengali primer *Borno Porichoy*. **Prarthana Samaj (1867**, Atmaram Pandurang; **M.G. Ranade**, Bhandarkar) worked for theistic worship and social reform in Bombay. **Swami Dayanand Saraswati** founded the **Arya Samaj (1875)** — 'Back to the Vedas', **shuddhi** (reconversion), DAV education. **Swami Vivekananda** founded the **Ramakrishna Mission (1897)** (Chicago address 1893) on service. The **Theosophical Society** (1875, New York; **Blavatsky & Olcott**; Indian HQ **Adyar, 1882**) found its Indian voice in **Annie Besant**. **Sir Syed Ahmed Khan** began the Aligarh movement — **MAO College (1875)**, later Aligarh Muslim University — for modern education among Muslims. The **Deccan Education Society (1884**, Tilak-Agarkar, Fergusson College) and **Gokhale's Servants of India Society (1905)** trained public workers.

### Lower-caste and regional assertions
**Jyotirao and Savitribai Phule** — Satyashodhak Samaj (**1873**) and Pune's first girls' school (1848). **Sri Narayana Guru** (Kerala) — the Ezhava reformer who consecrated the Aruvippuram Shiva shrine (1888) and inspired the **SNDP Yogam (1903)** — 'one caste, one religion, one God for man'. **Periyar E.V. Ramaswamy** launched the **Self-Respect Movement (1925)** in Tamil country for caste and gender equality. **Sikh revival** — the Singh Sabha (1873, Amritsar). In Maharashtra, **Gopal Baba Walangkar** and later **Shahu Maharaj** pushed reserved seats and caste reform; B.R. Ambedkar's **Mahad Satyagraha (1927)** opened the struggle for untouchable rights.

### The legislation timeline
**1829** sati abolished (Regulation XVII) · **1856** widow remarriage legal · **1891** Age of Consent Act (raised to 12) · **1929** Child Marriage Restraint (**Sarda**) Act — marriage age 18 (boys) and 14 (girls).

### Quick revision
- Roy-Brahmo 1828-sati; Vidyasagar-Widow Remarriage Act 1856; Prarthana 1867-Ranade; Arya 1875-Dayanand.
- Ramakrishna Mission 1897-Vivekananda; Theosophy 1875 (Adyar) - Besant; Aligarh-MAO 1875-Sir Syed.
- Phule-Satyashodhak 1873; Narayana Guru-SNDP-Kerala; Periyar-Self-Respect 1925.
- Law years: sati 1829, remarriage 1856, consent 1891, Sarda 1929.

subtopics.notes:
### The Congress is born (1885)
A retired ICS officer, **A.O. Hume**, brought 72 Indian delegates together at **Bombay** (Gokuldas Tejpal Sanskrit College) in **December 1885** — the first session of the **Indian National Congress**. Its first president was **W.C. Bonnerjee**. The "safety-valve" reading — that Hume wanted a yearly talking-shop to let out discontent — was argued by **Lala Lajpat Rai** in his book *Young India*; modern historians see it as the first all-India political platform.

### The Moderates (1885–1905)
Leaders: **Dadabhai Naoroji** (thrice president; first Indian MP in the British House of Commons, 1892; the 'Grand Old Man of India'), **S.N. Banerjea** (Indian Association, 1876; paper *Bengalee*), **Gokhale** (Servants of India Society, 1905; Gandhi's political guru), **Pherozeshah Mehta** ('Lion of Bombay'), **R.C. Dutt** (*Economic History of India*). Methods: petitions, prayers and protests — the '3P' path — trusting British justice. Their lasting contribution was **economic criticism**: Naoroji's **Drain of Wealth** theory (*Poverty and Un-British Rule in India*, 1901) showed how India's money flowed out as salaries, pensions and profits.

### Extremists (1905–1919)
**Lal-Bal-Pal** — **Lala Lajpat Rai** (Punjab Kesari), **Bal Gangadhar Tilak**, **Bipin Chandra Pal** — plus **Aurobindo Ghosh**. Tilak ran **Kesari** (Marathi) and *Mahratta* (English), started the **Ganapati (1893)** and **Shivaji (1895)** festivals, and declared **"Swaraj is my birthright and I shall have it."** Jailed for six years (1908–14) in **Mandalay**, where he wrote *Geeta Rahasya*. They wanted self-rule, not petitions, and believed in mass action, swadeshi and national education.

### Partition of Bengal (1905) and Swadeshi
**Lord Curzon** partitioned Bengal (effective **16 October 1905**) on the plea of administrative convenience — really to break Bengali nationalism: a Muslim-majority **East Bengal and Assam**, a Hindu-majority west. The answer was the **Swadeshi movement**: boycott of foreign cloth and salt, **Rakhi bandhan** (Tagore's idea), *Amar Sonar Bangla* as the marching song, national schools (the **National Council of Education, 1906**) and volunteer samitis. The partition was **annulled in 1911**.

### Split, League, reforms, reunion
- **Surat, 1907**: the session split — Moderates (Rash Behari Ghosh) vs Extremists (Tilak). The two wings **reunited at Lucknow in 1916**.
- **Muslim League, 1906**: founded at **Dacca** (Nawab Salimullah's initiative); it backed the partition and soon demanded **separate electorates**.
- **Calcutta session, 1906** (Naoroji president): the word **Swaraj** entered the Congress resolution.
- **Morley-Minto reforms, 1909**: first Indians in the executive councils (Satyendra P. Sinha), but also **separate electorates** for Muslims — Minto is called the father of communal electorates.
- **Home Rule Leagues, 1916**: Tilak's (April, Maharashtra-Karnataka-CP-Berar) and **Annie Besant's** (September, Madras; papers *New India* and *Commonweal*); Besant became Congress president in 1917.

### Quick revision
- INC 1885, Bombay, Hume; first president W.C. Bonnerjee; 72 delegates.
- Moderates: Naoroji (drain theory), Gokhale, S.N. Banerjea, Mehta, R.C. Dutt.
- Tilak: Kesari + Mahratta, Ganapati 1893, Mandalay 1908–14, Home Rule 1916.
- Curzon's partition 1905 → Swadeshi → annulled 1911; Surat split 1907, Lucknow reunion 1916.
- League 1906 Dacca; Morley-Minto 1909 = separate electorates.

subtopics.notes:
### Gandhi arrives (1915)
Mohandas Karamchand Gandhi — a barrister who had forged the **satyagraha** (truth-force, passive resistance) method in South Africa from 1906 — landed in India on **9 January 1915**. Three local struggles taught India the method:
- **Champaran, 1917** (Bihar): against the forced indigo cultivation and the **tinkathia** system; **Rajkumar Shukla** brought Gandhi; his **first satyagraha in India**.
- **Ahmedabad mill strike, 1918**: for mill workers' plague bonus — his **first hunger strike**.
- **Kheda, 1918** (Gujarat): **no-revenue** campaign for famine-hit peasants, organised with **Sardar Vallabhbhai Patel**.

### 1919: Rowlatt, Jallianwala, Khilafat
The **Rowlatt Act (1919)** allowed detention without trial — 'no dalil, no vakil, no appeal'. The **Jallianwala Bagh massacre (13 April 1919)**, Amritsar: General **Dyer** fired on an unarmed Baisakhi crowd; **Rabindranath Tagore** returned his knighthood; **Udham Singh** shot Michael O'Dwyer in London (1940). The **Khilafat movement** (Ali brothers) against the Ottoman Caliphate's treatment folded into Gandhi's **Non-Cooperation Movement (1920–22)**: boycott of schools, courts, titles and foreign cloth. It was withdrawn in **February 1922** after violence at **Chauri Chaura** (Gorakhpur). The **Swaraj Party (1923)** — C.R. Das and Motilal Nehru — entered councils instead.

### From Simon to Purna Swaraj
The all-white **Simon Commission (arrived 1928)** was met with 'Go back Simon'; **Lala Lajpat Rai** was fatally injured in its Lahore lathi charge. The **Nehru Report (1928)** — Motilal Nehru — was India's first constitution draft. At **Lahore (December 1929)**, with **Jawaharlal Nehru** as president, Congress declared **Purna Swaraj**; **26 January 1930** was observed as Independence Day.

### Civil Disobedience (1930–34)
Gandhi marched **12 March 1930** from Sabarmati with 78 followers to **Dandi**, breaking the salt law on **6 April 1930**. The **Gandhi-Irwin Pact (5 March 1931)** ended the phase; Gandhi went alone to the **Second Round Table Conference (1931)**. The **Communal Award (1932)** gave separate electorates to the Depressed Classes; the **Poona Pact (September 1932)** with **Ambedkar** replaced them with reserved seats under joint electorates. The **Government of India Act, 1935** gave provincial autonomy — Congress ministries ruled 1937–39.

### 1942–47: Quit India and freedom
Rejecting the **Cripps offer (1942)** — Gandhi's 'post-dated cheque on a crashing bank' — Congress passed the **Quit India resolution on 8 August 1942** at Gowalia Tank, Bombay: **'Do or Die'**. The leaders were arrested at once; **Aruna Asaf Ali** hoisted the flag, **Usha Mehta** ran the Congress Radio; parallel governments rose at **Ballia (Chittu Pandey), Satara (Nana Patil) and Tamluk**. Meanwhile **Subhas Chandra Bose** revived the **INA** (Azad Hind government, Singapore, 1943; 'Dilli Chalo'; 'Give me blood, I will give you freedom'; Rani Jhansi Regiment — Lakshmi Sahgal). The **Cabinet Mission (1946)** — Pethick-Lawrence, Cripps, Alexander — planned the transfer; after **Direct Action Day (16 August 1946)** and the **Mountbatten Plan (3 June 1947)**, power was transferred on **15 August 1947**.

### Quick revision
- First satyagraha in India: Champaran 1917 (tinkathia, Rajkumar Shukla); then Ahmedabad 1918, Kheda 1918.
- 1919: Rowlatt Act → Jallianwala (Dyer, 13 April) → Tagore's knighthood back.
- NCM 1920–22 ends at Chauri Chaura; Swaraj Party 1923 (Das, Motilal).
- Lahore 1929 (Jawaharlal) → 26 Jan 1930 → Dandi (12 Mar–6 Apr 1930) → Gandhi-Irwin 1931 → Poona Pact 1932.
- 1942: Quit India, 'Do or Die'; Bose: Azad Hind 1943; 1946 Cabinet Mission; 15 Aug 1947.

subtopics.notes:
### Why the press mattered
The national movement ran on print. Newspapers created all-India opinion, spread boycott calls, and paid for it with prosecution. Know the paper, its editor and its language — that trio is the whole question bank.

### Early national press
**Raja Ram Mohan Roy** was the pioneer: *Sambad Kaumudi* (Bengali, 1821) and *Mirat-ul-Akbar* (Persian, 1822). **Amrita Bazar Patrika** (1868, the Ghosh brothers — Sisir Kumar and Motilal) began in Bengali; when the **Vernacular Press Act (1878)** gagged Indian-language papers, it converted itself into an English daily **overnight**. *The Hindu* (Madras, 1878) was founded by **G. Subramania Iyer**. **Surendranath Banerjea** edited *Bengalee*; *Kesari* (Marathi) and *Mahratta* (English), both 1881, were **Tilak's** platforms. The **Vernacular Press Act (1878)** — Lytton's 'Gagging Act' — was repealed by **Ripon in 1882**; earlier, **Metcalfe (1835)** had earned the title 'liberator of the Indian press'.

### Papers of the freedom struggle
**Gandhi**: *Young India* (English) and *Navajivan* (Gujarati) during NCM; *Harijan* (1933) for the anti-untouchability work. **Annie Besant**: *New India* and *Commonweal*. **Maulana Azad**: Urdu *Al-Hilal* (1912) and *Al-Balagh*. **Muhammad Ali** (of the Ali brothers): *Comrade*. **Aurobindo Ghosh**: *Bande Mataram*; **Bipin Chandra Pal** worked on it too. Sir Syed's *Tahdhib-ul-Akhlaq* carried the Aligarh message.

### The books to memorise
| Book | Author |
|---|---|
| *Poverty and Un-British Rule in India* (1901) | Dadabhai Naoroji |
| *Economic History of India* | R.C. Dutt |
| *Hind Swaraj* (1909) | Gandhi |
| *My Experiments with Truth* (autobiography, 1927) | Gandhi |
| *Geeta Rahasya* (in Mandalay jail) | Tilak |
| *Ghulamgiri* (1873) | Jyotiba Phule |
| *Annihilation of Caste* (1936) | B.R. Ambedkar |
| *The Indian Struggle* (1935) | Subhas Chandra Bose |
| *Toward Freedom* (autobiography, 1936) | Jawaharlal Nehru |
| *Glimpses of World History* (1934) | Jawaharlal Nehru |
| *Discovery of India* (1946) | Jawaharlal Nehru |
| *India Wins Freedom* | Maulana Abul Kalam Azad |
| *India Divided* | Rajendra Prasad |
| *Unhappy India* (1928) | Lala Lajpat Rai |

### Songs and symbols from print
**Bankim Chandra Chatterjee's** novel *Anandamath* (1882) gave the song **Vande Mataram**, first sung at the **1896 Calcutta Congress session** by Rabindranath Tagore. Tagore's *Amar Sonar Bangla* was written during the 1905 Swadeshi agitation.

### Quick revision
- Roy: Sambad Kaumudi (Bengali) + Mirat-ul-Akbar (Persian).
- Amrita Bazar Patrika: Ghosh brothers; turned English overnight after the 1878 Act.
- Gandhi: Young India, Navajivan, Harijan (1933). Besant: New India, Commonweal. Azad: Al-Hilal.
- Naoroji: Poverty and Un-British Rule; Dutt: Economic History; Bose: Indian Struggle.
- Nehru: Toward Freedom, Glimpses, Discovery; Azad: India Wins Freedom.

patterns.name: Newspaper ↔ editor/founder
patterns.howToSpot: 'Who edited Kesari', 'New India was published by', match-the-column of papers and editors.
patterns.logic:
1. Tilak = *Kesari* + *Mahratta*; Besant = *New India* + *Commonweal*; Gandhi = *Young India* + *Navajivan* + *Harijan*.
2. Azad = *Al-Hilal*; Muhammad Ali = *Comrade*; S.N. Banerjea = *Bengalee*; Aurobindo = *Bande Mataram*.
3. Watch the near-pair: *New India* is Besant's paper — not Pal's, not Nehru's.

example.q: The newspaper ***New India***, which carried the Home Rule campaign, was started by —
example.solution: **Annie Besant** — her other paper was *Commonweal*.

patterns.name: Book ↔ author
patterns.howToSpot: 'Who wrote Discovery of India', 'Ghulamgiri is a work by', match-the-column of books and authors.
patterns.logic:

2. Economic pair: Naoroji (*Poverty and Un-British Rule*) vs R.C. Dutt (*Economic History of India*).
3. Azad = *India Wins Freedom*; Prasad = *India Divided*; Bose = *The Indian Struggle*; Ambedkar = *Annihilation of Caste*.

example.q: The book ***Discovery of India*** was written by —
example.solution: **Jawaharlal Nehru**, during his Ahmednagar prison years (1946).

patterns.name: Press laws: 1878 Act and press freedom

patterns.logic:
1. **Vernacular Press Act, 1878** — Lord **Lytton**; repealed by **Ripon, 1882**.
2. **Amrita Bazar Patrika** turned into an English paper overnight to escape it.
3. **Metcalfe (1835)** = 'liberator of the Indian press'.

example.q: The **Vernacular Press Act (1878)** was repealed by —
example.solution: **Lord Ripon**, in 1882.

patterns.name: Gandhi's journals
patterns.howToSpot: 'Harijan was started in', which paper during Non-Cooperation, language of Navajivan.
patterns.logic:
1. NCM years: *Young India* (English) and *Navajivan* (Gujarati).
2. ***Harijan*** (1933): English weekly for the anti-untouchability campaign; sister papers *Harijan Bandhu* (Gujarati), *Harijan Sevak* (Hindi).
3. *Indian Opinion* (1903) was Gandhi's South African paper.

example.q: Gandhi started the English weekly ***Harijan*** in —
example.solution: **1933**, for the removal of untouchability.

patterns.name: Anandamath, Vande Mataram and protest writings
patterns.howToSpot: Source of Vande Mataram, where it was first sung, Amar Sonar Bangla's origin, Unhappy India as a reply to Mother India.
patterns.logic:
1. *Anandamath* (1882) by **Bankim Chandra Chatterjee** contains **Vande Mataram**; first sung by **Tagore** at the **1896 Calcutta Congress**.
2. Tagore's ***Amar Sonar Bangla*** (1905 Swadeshi) later became Bangladesh's anthem.
3. Lajpat Rai's *Unhappy India* (1928) answered Katherine Mayo's *Mother India*.

example.q: The song ***Vande Mataram*** first appeared in —
example.solution: Bankim Chandra Chatterjee's novel ***Anandamath*** (1882).

pyqPatterns.howToSpot: Arrange 3–4 events in order, or 'which happened first/last'. The single most repeated modern-history ask, from Plassey to independence.
pyqPatterns.approach: Fix anchor years once (1757, 1857, 1885, 1905, 1919, 1930, 1942, 1947) and slot each event against them; never rely on 'feel' — place the two events you are sure of and the order falls out.

example.q: Arrange: (1) Jallianwala Bagh (2) Chauri Chaura (3) Dandi March (4) Quit India.

pyqPatterns.howToSpot: 'Who was the Governor-General when…', 'the Doctrine of Lapse was applied by', or a match-the-column of Viceroys and events.
pyqPatterns.approach: Memorise the spine: Cornwallis (judicial), Bentinck (social reforms, sati), Dalhousie (annexations, railways), Lytton (press gag), Ripon (local self-government), Curzon (partition of Bengal), Minto (Morley-Minto). Each Viceroy owns 1–2 tag facts.

example.q: Under which Governor-General was the **Doctrine of Lapse** used to annex princely states?
example.solution: **Dalhousie** (1848–56) — Satara, Jhansi, Nagpur and others annexed by refusing adopted heirs.

pyqPatterns.howToSpot: A centre (Kanpur, Lucknow, Jhansi, Bareilly…) is named and its leader asked, often as match-the-column.
pyqPatterns.approach: Six pairs settle it: Delhi–Bahadur Shah II, Kanpur–Nana Saheb, Lucknow–Begum Hazrat Mahal, Jhansi–Rani Lakshmibai, Bareilly–Khan Bahadur Khan, Bihar (Jagdishpur)–Kunwar Singh.

example.q: Who led the 1857 revolt at **Kanpur**?
example.solution: **Nana Saheb** — with Tantia Tope as his commander and the seized treasury; Lucknow belongs to Begum Hazrat Mahal, not him.

pyqPatterns.howToSpot: 'The Lahore session of 1929 was presided over by', 'Purna Swaraj was declared at…', or the session where a famous word entered the resolution.
pyqPatterns.approach: Pin the famous sessions: 1885 Bombay (Bonnerjee), 1906 Calcutta (Naoroji — 'Swaraj'), 1907 Surat (split), 1916 Lucknow (reunion), 1929 Lahore (Jawaharlal — Purna Swaraj), 1931 Karachi (Fundamental Rights), 1942 (Quit India, AICC).

example.q: At which session did the Congress resolve to strive for **'Swaraj'** (1906)?
example.solution: The **Calcutta session of 1906**, with Dadabhai Naoroji in the chair.

pyqPatterns.howToSpot: 'Kesari was edited by', 'Discovery of India was written by', and match-the-column sets mixing papers and books in one question.
pyqPatterns.approach: Cluster by person: Tilak (Kesari, Mahratta, Geeta Rahasya), Gandhi (Young India, Navajivan, Harijan, Hind Swaraj, Experiments), Nehru (Toward Freedom, Glimpses, Discovery), Naoroji vs R.C. Dutt for the two economics books.

example.q: The author of ***India Wins Freedom*** is —
example.solution: **Maulana Abul Kalam Azad** — Rajendra Prasad wrote *India Divided*; don't swap the pair.

pyqPatterns.howToSpot: Statements about a movement (its trigger, methods, where it spread, why it ended) with 'which is/are correct'.
pyqPatterns.approach: For each movement fix four anchors — trigger event, signature method, geographic spread, end event. Example, Civil Disobedience: salt law broken at Dandi, no-revenue/no-tax, spread widest in Gujarat and Tamil belt, ended by the Gandhi-Irwin Pact.

example.q: The Civil Disobedience Movement was launched in 1930 by —
example.solution: Breaking the **salt law at Dandi** (6 April 1930), after the 12 March march from Sabarmati.

pyqPatterns.howToSpot: 'Swaraj is my birthright' — who said it, 'Do or Die', 'Give me blood', 'Dilli Chalo', and other one-line attributions.
pyqPatterns.approach: Attribute by decade and method: Tilak (birthright), Gandhi (Do or Die, the three monkeys), Bose (Dilli Chalo, Give me blood), Bhagat Singh (Inquilab Zindabad popularised), Nehru (the tryst with destiny, 1947).

example.q: 'Give me blood, I will give you freedom' was said by —
example.solution: **Subhas Chandra Bose**, to the INA in 1944.

pyqPatterns.howToSpot: 'The Brahmo Samaj was founded by', statements on widow remarriage, sati abolition, Aligarh movement, and their year-provision mix.
pyqPatterns.approach: Track reformer → society → year: Ram Mohan Roy (Brahmo Sabha 1828, sati abolished 1829 with Bentinck), Dayananda (Arya Samaj 1875), Ramakrishna–Vivekananda (Mission 1897), Syed Ahmad Khan (MAO College 1875), Phule (Satyashodhak Samaj 1873).

example.q: The practice of **sati** was legally abolished in 1829 through the efforts of —
example.solution: **Raja Ram Mohan Roy**, whose campaign persuaded Lord William Bentinck to pass the regulation.

solvedExamples.q:
Arrange the following in chronological order:
1. Rowlatt Satyagraha
2. Arrival of the Simon Commission
3. Champaran Satyagraha
4. Gandhi–Irwin Pact
solvedExamples.solution: Champaran **1917** → Rowlatt Satyagraha **1919** → Simon Commission **1928** → Gandhi–Irwin Pact **1931**. Order: 3, 1, 2, 4.
solvedExamples.shortcut: Champaran is Gandhi's first satyagraha in India, so it must come first → only A and C remain; Rowlatt (1919) is before Simon (1928) → A.

solvedExamples.q: Which of the following pairs of Governor-General/Viceroy and measure is **NOT** correctly matched?
options: Lord Canning — First Viceroy of India
solvedExamples.solution: The **Ilbert Bill (1883)**, which allowed Indian judges to try Europeans, came under **Lord Ripon**. Curzon is linked with the partition of Bengal (1905). The other three pairs are correct.
solvedExamples.shortcut: Ripon is the 'liberal' Viceroy — both the local self-government resolution and the Ilbert Bill belong to him.

solvedExamples.q: Begum Hazrat Mahal led the Revolt of 1857 at —
solvedExamples.solution: **Begum Hazrat Mahal** of Awadh led the rising at **Lucknow** and proclaimed her son Birjis Qadr ruler. Kanpur – Nana Saheb; Jhansi – Rani Lakshmibai; Faizabad – Maulvi Ahmadullah.

solvedExamples.q: The resolution on **Fundamental Rights and Economic Policy** was adopted by the Indian National Congress at its 1931 session held at —
solvedExamples.solution: The **Karachi session (March 1931)**, presided over by **Vallabhbhai Patel**, adopted the resolution on Fundamental Rights and National Economic Programme and endorsed the Gandhi–Irwin Pact. Lahore (1929) adopted Purna Swaraj.

practice.q: The **Battle of Plassey**, in which Robert Clive defeated Siraj-ud-Daulah, was fought in —
practice.solution: Plassey was fought on **23 June 1757**. 1764 = Buxar; 1761 = Third Panipat; 1799 = death of Tipu Sultan.

practice.q: The **Diwani** of Bengal, Bihar and Orissa was granted to the East India Company by the —
practice.solution: After Buxar, Mughal emperor Shah Alam II granted the Diwani (right to collect revenue) through the **Treaty of Allahabad (1765)**. Salbai (1782) ended the First Anglo-Maratha War; Srirangapatna (1792) the Third Anglo-Mysore War.

practice.q: The **Subsidiary Alliance** system was introduced by —
practice.solution: **Lord Wellesley** (1798–1805) made Indian rulers keep British troops at their own cost and accept a British Resident; the Nizam of Hyderabad signed first (1798).

practice.q: The **Permanent Settlement** of land revenue in Bengal (1793) was introduced by —
practice.solution: **Lord Cornwallis** fixed revenue permanently with the zamindars in 1793. It is also called the Zamindari system.

practice.q: The practice of **sati** was declared illegal in 1829 during the tenure of —
practice.solution: The **Bengal Sati Regulation (Regulation XVII) of 1829** was passed by **Lord William Bentinck**, supported by the campaign of Raja Ram Mohan Roy.

practice.q: Who led the Revolt of 1857 at **Kanpur**?
practice.solution: **Nana Saheb**, adopted son of Peshwa Baji Rao II, led the revolt at Kanpur with Tantia Tope. Kunwar Singh – Jagdishpur (Bihar); Begum Hazrat Mahal – Lucknow; Khan Bahadur Khan – Bareilly.

practice.q: The **Arya Samaj** was founded in 1875 by —
practice.solution: **Swami Dayanand Saraswati** founded the Arya Samaj in **Bombay (1875)**. He wrote *Satyarth Prakash* and gave the call 'Back to the Vedas'.

practice.q: The **Satyashodhak Samaj** (1873), which worked for the rights of the lower castes, was founded by —
practice.solution: **Jyotirao Phule** founded the Satyashodhak Samaj ('Society of Truth-seekers') in 1873 in Maharashtra and wrote *Gulamgiri* the same year.
practice.shortcut: **P**hule = **P**eople of the lower castes; year **1873** = Gulamgiri year.

practice.q: The **Partition of Bengal** (1905) was carried out by which Viceroy?
practice.solution: **Lord Curzon** announced the partition, which took effect on **16 October 1905** and triggered the Swadeshi movement. It was annulled in **1911** under Lord Hardinge.

practice.q: The Indian National Congress split into Moderates and Extremists at its session held at **Surat** in —
practice.solution: The **Surat split** took place in **December 1907**. The two groups reunited at Lucknow in **1916**.
practice.shortcut: 5-6-**7**-9: Bengal split, League, **Congress split**, separate electorates.

practice.q: The **Champaran Satyagraha** (1917), Gandhi's first satyagraha in India, took place in present-day —
practice.solution: Champaran is in **Bihar**. Gandhi went there on Raj Kumar Shukla's request to take up the grievances of indigo cultivators under the **tinkathia** system.
practice.shortcut: **C**hamparan = first letter of the chain C-A-K; indigo in Bihar.

practice.q: Who renounced his knighthood in protest against the **Jallianwala Bagh massacre** of 1919?
practice.solution: **Rabindranath Tagore** gave up the knighthood conferred on him in 1915 by writing to the Viceroy (Lord Chelmsford) in May 1919. Gandhi later returned his Kaiser-i-Hind medal.
practice.shortcut: Only a 'Sir' could renounce a knighthood → Sir Rabindranath.

practice.q: The **Purna Swaraj** resolution was adopted at the Lahore session of the Congress (1929) presided over by —
practice.solution: **Jawaharlal Nehru** presided over the **Lahore session (December 1929)**, which declared complete independence as the goal; 26 January 1930 was celebrated as Independence Day.

practice.q: Gandhi began the **Dandi March** from Sabarmati Ashram on —
practice.solution: The march started on **12 March 1930** and reached Dandi, where Gandhi broke the salt law on **6 April 1930**. 5 March 1931 is the Gandhi–Irwin Pact.
practice.shortcut: **12** March start, **6** April finish — start is always the March date.

practice.q: The **Poona Pact (1932)** on the representation of the depressed classes was signed between —
practice.solution: After the **Communal Award** (1932), Gandhi fasted in Yerawada jail. The **Poona Pact** with **B.R. Ambedkar** replaced separate electorates for the depressed classes with reserved seats in joint electorates.

practice.q: The slogan **'Do or Die'** was given by Gandhi during the —
practice.solution: Gandhi gave the call 'Do or Die' on **8 August 1942** at **Gowalia Tank, Bombay**, when the Quit India resolution was passed.
practice.shortcut: 1942 = last big push → last-chance slogan 'Do or Die'.

practice.q: The headquarters of the **Ghadar Party** (Yugantar Ashram) was located in —
practice.solution: The Ghadar Party (1913), led by **Lala Har Dayal** and **Sohan Singh Bhakna**, was run from **Yugantar Ashram in San Francisco**, USA, and published the weekly *Ghadar*.
practice.shortcut: Ghadar = Indians on the **US Pacific coast** → San Francisco.

practice.q: Subhas Chandra Bose proclaimed the **Provisional Government of Free India (Azad Hind)** on 21 October 1943 at —
practice.solution: The Azad Hind Government was proclaimed in **Singapore**. The INA's HQ later moved to Rangoon; Bose had earlier worked from Berlin.

practice.q: The Urdu weekly ***Al-Hilal*** (1912) was started by —
practice.solution: **Maulana Abul Kalam Azad** launched *Al-Hilal* from Calcutta in 1912. Mohammad Ali Jauhar edited *Comrade*.

practice.q: The **Battle of Buxar** was fought in —
practice.solution: **Buxar, 1764**: the Company's army under Hector Munro defeated the combined forces of Mir Qasim, Shuja-ud-Daula and Shah Alam II.

practice.q: The first **Governor-General of Bengal** (under the Regulating Act, 1773) was —
practice.solution: **Warren Hastings** became Governor-General of Bengal in 1773; the title 'Governor-General of India' began with William Bentinck (1833).
practice.shortcut: Hastings first GG; Bentinck first 'of India'.

practice.q: Tipu Sultan is called the **'Tiger of Mysore'**. He was killed in —
practice.solution: Tipu died defending his capital **Srirangapatna** in the **Fourth Anglo-Mysore War (1799)** under Lord Wellesley.

practice.q: Under the **Doctrine of Lapse**, whose adoption claim as heir was rejected, leading to annexation?
practice.solution: **Dalhousie's Doctrine of Lapse** refused recognition to adopted heirs — Jhansi (Lakshmibai), Satara, Nagpur and others lapsed. Nana Saheb's pension claim was refused too.

practice.q: **English** was made the medium of higher education in India (Macaulay's Minute, 1835) under —
practice.solution: **Bentinck** accepted **Macaulay's Minute (1835)**, making English the medium of higher education; he also abolished sati (1829).

practice.q:
Consider the statements:
1. The Vernacular Press Act was passed in 1878.
2. The Delhi Durbar of 1877 proclaimed Victoria 'Empress of India'.
3. The Arms Act of Lytton's time disarmed Indians.
Which are correct?
practice.solution: All three belong to **Lytton's** tenure (1876–80): the press gag (1878), the 1877 Durbar, and the Arms Act.
practice.shortcut: Lytton's trio: press gag, Arms Act, Durbar.

practice.q: In the **Mahalwari** system, the unit of settlement was —
practice.solution: **Mahalwari** settlement was made with the **village estate** as a whole (North-Western Provinces, Central India, parts of Punjab), following Holt Mackenzie's 1822 rules.

practice.q:
Match:
1. Permanent Settlement — Cornwallis
2. Ryotwari — Thomas Munro
3. Mahalwari — Lord Wellesley
Which pairs are correct?
practice.solution: **Cornwallis** (Permanent Settlement) and **Munro** (Ryotwari) are right; **Mahalwari** is associated with **Holt Mackenzie**, not Wellesley.
practice.shortcut: Wellesley belongs to Subsidiary Alliance — a classic distractor.

practice.q: Who led the Revolt of 1857 at **Jhansi**?
practice.solution: **Rani Lakshmibai** fought for Jhansi (her adopted heir was refused under the Doctrine of Lapse) and died at Gwalior in June 1858.

practice.q: **Kunwar Singh**, the aged leader of the 1857 revolt, was associated with —
practice.solution: **Kunwar Singh** of Jagdishpur, near Arrah in Bihar, fought the British through 1857-58.

practice.q:
Match:
1. Bareilly — Khan Bahadur Khan
2. Faizabad — Maulvi Ahmadullah Shah
3. Gwalior — Bakht Khan
Which are correct?
practice.solution: Bareilly-**Khan Bahadur Khan** and Faizabad-**Ahmadullah Shah** are right; **Bakht Khan** was the rebel general at **Delhi**, not Gwalior.
practice.shortcut: Gwalior belongs to the Rani; Bakht Khan to Delhi.

practice.q: The **immediate cause** of the Revolt of 1857 was —
practice.solution: The new **Enfield rifle cartridges**, rumoured greased with cow and pig fat, sparked the revolt — the deeper causes were political, economic and military.

practice.q: **Mangal Pandey** belonged to which regiment?
practice.solution: Mangal Pandey of the **34th Native Infantry** attacked officers at **Barrackpore** on 29 March 1857; the regiment was disbanded.

practice.q: The annexation of **Awadh in 1856** was justified by the British on the ground of —
practice.solution: **Awadh** was annexed in **1856** on grounds of 'misgovernment' — not Lapse. The annexation alienated the talukdars and sepoys (many were from Awadh).
practice.shortcut: Lapse for adopted heirs; Awadh = misgovernment.

practice.q: The Revolt of 1857 **broke out in full** at Meerut on —
practice.solution: On **10 May 1857** the Meerut sepoys mutinied and marched to Delhi, proclaiming Bahadur Shah II. (29 March = Barrackpore/Mangal Pandey.)

practice.q: After the fall of Delhi (1857), **Bahadur Shah II** was —
practice.solution: The old emperor was tried at Delhi and **exiled to Rangoon**, where he died in 1862; his sons were shot by Captain Hodson.

practice.q:
Consider the statements:
1. The Act of 1858 created the office of Secretary of State for India.
2. Canning became the first Viceroy.
3. The Queen's Proclamation was issued at Allahabad.
Which are correct?
practice.solution: All three are standard outcomes of 1858: the Secretary of State (with a 15-member Council), **Canning** as first Viceroy, and the **Proclamation at Allahabad** (1 November 1858).
practice.shortcut: The 1858 package: SoS + Viceroy + Allahabad Proclamation.

practice.q: The **Paika rebellion (1817)** of Odisha was led by —
practice.solution: **Bakshi Jagabandhu Bidyadhar**, the Paika (soldier-landholder) chief of Khurda, led the 1817 rebellion against British land and revenue changes.

practice.q: **Birsa Munda's** Ulgulan (1899-1900) was aimed at —
options: Driving out the British and outsiders from tribal land
practice.solution: The **Ulgulan** ('Great Tumult') of the Munda tribes demanded self-rule of tribal lands; its aftermath included the **Chotanagpur Tenancy Act (1908)**.

practice.q: Which pair of uprising and leader is **incorrectly** matched?
practice.solution: The **Moplahs are Muslim peasants of Malabar**, not Paikas (the Paikas are Odisha's soldier-landholders of the 1817 rebellion). The other three pairs are correct.

practice.q: The **Brahmo Samaj** was founded in 1828 by —
practice.solution: **Ram Mohan Roy** founded the Brahmo Sabha (later Samaj) in **1828** — preaching monotheism and against idol worship.

practice.q: The **Ramakrishna Mission** was founded in 1897 by —
practice.solution: **Vivekananda** founded the Ramakrishna Mission (1897) in his guru Ramakrishna's name — its motto: service to man as service to God.

practice.q: The **Mohammedan Anglo-Oriental (MAO) College** of 1875, which became Aligarh Muslim University, was founded by —
practice.solution: **Sir Syed Ahmed Khan** founded MAO College (1875) — the heart of the Aligarh movement for modern education among Muslims.

practice.q: Who opened one of the first **girls' schools** in Pune in 1848?
practice.solution: **Savitribai Phule**, taught by and working with **Jyotirao Phule**, ran the pioneering girls' school at Bhide Wada, Pune (1848).

practice.q: The **Theosophical Society**'s international headquarters at **Adyar** (1882) is near which city?
practice.solution: The Theosophical Society (founded 1875 in New York by **Blavatsky and Olcott**) moved its headquarters to **Adyar, Madras**, in 1882; Annie Besant led it later.

practice.q: **Servants of India Society** (1905), which trained dedicated public workers, was founded by —
practice.solution: **Gokhale** founded the Servants of India Society in 1905 — he was also Gandhi's acknowledged political guru.

practice.q: The **Hindu Widows' Remarriage Act** was passed in —
practice.solution: The **Widows' Remarriage Act (1856)** legalised widow remarriage — Vidyasagar's campaign. Sati was banned in 1829.

practice.q:
Arrange the reform laws chronologically:
1. Sarda Act  2. Sati abolition  3. Age of Consent Act  4. Widow Remarriage Act
practice.solution: **Sati (1829) → Widow Remarriage (1856) → Age of Consent (1891) → Sarda Act (1929)**.

practice.q: The **Age of Consent Act, 1891** raised the age of consent for girls to —
practice.solution: The **Age of Consent Act (1891)** raised it from 10 to **12** years — passed after the Rukhmabai and Phulmoni controversies.

practice.q: **Sri Narayana Guru**, who consecrated the Aruvippuram temple (1888), worked among the —
practice.solution: **Sri Narayana Guru** led the Ezhava reform movement in Kerala and inspired the **SNDP Yogam (1903)**.

practice.q: Which reform movement's motto was **'one caste, one religion, one God for man'**?
options: The movement of Sri Narayana Guru
practice.solution: **Sri Narayana Guru's** famous formulation summarised his anti-caste universalism in Kerala.

practice.q:
Consider the statements:
1. Arya Samaj launched shuddhi (reconversion) ceremonies.
2. The Singh Sabha (1873) worked for Sikh revival.
3. The Mahad Satyagraha (1927) was led by Periyar.
Which are correct?
practice.solution: Statements 1 and 2 are right. The **Mahad Satyagraha was led by B.R. Ambedkar**, not Periyar (whose movement is the Self-Respect Movement).

practice.q: The **Indian National Congress** was founded in 1885 by —
practice.solution: **Alan Octavian Hume**, a retired ICS officer, organised the first session at Bombay in December 1885; **W.C. Bonnerjee** presided.

practice.q: How many delegates attended the **first session** of the Indian National Congress?
practice.solution: The Bombay session of **December 1885** had **72 delegates**, drawn mostly from professional classes of the presidencies.

practice.q: Who is known as the **'Grand Old Man of India'**?
practice.solution: **Naoroji** — thrice Congress president, first Indian MP in the British House of Commons (1892), author of the drain theory.

practice.q:
Consider the statements about Moderate leaders:
1. Gokhale founded the Servants of India Society in 1905.
2. S.N. Banerjea founded the Indian Association in 1876.
3. R.C. Dutt wrote *Poverty and Un-British Rule in India*.
Which are correct?
practice.solution: *Poverty and Un-British Rule in India* is **Naoroji's** book; **R.C. Dutt** wrote the *Economic History of India*.
practice.shortcut: Swap the two economic books — that's the trap.

practice.q: Tilak started the public **Ganapati festival** in 1893 primarily to —
options: Build a mass base against British rule
practice.solution: The **Ganapati (1893)** and **Shivaji (1895)** festivals gave Tilak a legal platform to gather and mobilise the masses.
practice.shortcut: Festivals = political mobilisation under a religious cover.

practice.q: Tilak was sentenced to six years' imprisonment in 1908 and imprisoned at —
practice.solution: After the 1908 sedition trial over *Kesari* articles, Tilak served **1908–14 in Mandalay**, writing *Geeta Rahasya* there.

practice.q: The stated purpose of the **Partition of Bengal (1905)** was —
practice.solution: Curzon claimed the province was too big to govern; nationalists saw the real aim — splitting Bengali unity — and launched the Swadeshi movement.
practice.shortcut: Stated = administrative; real = divide the nationalists.

practice.q:
Match:
1. Rakhi bandhan as protest — Rabindranath Tagore
2. *Amar Sonar Bangla* — composed during Swadeshi agitation
3. National Council of Education — 1906
Which are correct?
practice.solution: All three are Swadeshi-era facts: Tagore's Rakhi tying and later the song (now Bangladesh's anthem), and the **National Council of Education (1906)** for national education.

practice.q: The Congress split into Moderates and Extremists took place at the **Surat session** of —
practice.solution: The **1907 Surat session** (Rash Behari Ghosh's presidency disputed) split the party; the wings reunited at **Lucknow in 1916**.

practice.q: At which Congress session were the **Moderates and Extremists reunited**?
practice.solution: The **Lucknow session (1916)** saw the reunion and the **Congress-League pact** (which accepted separate electorates).

practice.q: Who among the following was the **first Indian member of the Viceroy's Executive Council** (1909)?
practice.solution: The **Morley-Minto reforms (1909)** admitted **S.P. Sinha** (law member) to the Viceroy's Executive Council — and introduced separate electorates.
practice.shortcut: Sinha in; separate electorates in — both 1909.

practice.q:
Consider the statements about the **Home Rule Leagues (1916)**:
1. Tilak's league worked in Maharashtra, Karnataka, the Central Provinces and Berar.
2. Annie Besant's league had its headquarters at Adyar, Madras.
3. Both leagues demanded Dominion Status within the British Empire.
Which are correct?
practice.solution: All three hold: the two leagues divided the country between them (Tilak: April 1916; Besant: September 1916) and both pressed for self-government within the Empire.
practice.shortcut: Two leagues, one demand: Home Rule.

practice.q: Gandhi's **first satyagraha in India** was launched at —
practice.solution: **Champaran (Bihar), 1917**, against the tinkathia indigo system — Rajkumar Shukla had persuaded Gandhi to come.

practice.q: The **tinkathia system**, which Gandhi fought in 1917, obliged Champaran peasants to —
options: Grow indigo on 3/20 of their land
Provide free transport to indigo factories
practice.solution: **Tinkathia** forced each raiyat to cultivate indigo on the **three kathas in every twenty** of his best land.

practice.q:
Arrange chronologically:
1. Ahmedabad mill strike
2. Champaran Satyagraha
3. Kheda Satyagraha
4. Return of Gandhi to India
practice.solution: Returned **9 January 1915** → **Champaran 1917** → **Ahmedabad 1918** (mill) → **Kheda 1918** (revenue).
practice.shortcut: 15-17-18-18: return, Champaran, then the two 1918 fights.

practice.q: The **Jallianwala Bagh massacre** was carried out on the orders of —
practice.solution: Brigadier-General **Reginald Dyer** ordered the firing on 13 April 1919; O'Dwyer was the Punjab Governor — later shot dead by Udham Singh (1940).
practice.shortcut: Dyer fired; O'Dwyer backed — Udham Singh shot O'Dwyer.

practice.q: The **Rowlatt Act (1919)** is remembered as the act of —
practice.solution: The Rowlatt Act allowed arrest and detention **without trial** — no lawyer, no argument, no appeal — and was never actually used much before it was repealed.

practice.q: The **Non-Cooperation Movement** was formally withdrawn after the violence at —
practice.solution: At **Chauri Chaura (Gorakhpur), 5 February 1922**, a mob set a police station ablaze; Gandhi, committed to non-violence, called off the movement.

practice.q: The **Swaraj Party** (1923), which entered the councils, was founded by —
practice.solution: After NCM's withdrawal, **C.R. Das and Motilal Nehru** formed the Swaraj Party to fight councils from within.

practice.q: How many volunteers accompanied Gandhi on the **Dandi March**?
practice.solution: Gandhi left Sabarmati on **12 March 1930 with 78 followers**, covering about 240 miles to Dandi and breaking the salt law on **6 April 1930**.

practice.q:
Match:
1. Communal Award — Ramsay MacDonald, 1932
2. Poona Pact — reserved seats under joint electorates
3. Gandhi attended the First Round Table Conference
Which are correct?
practice.solution: Gandhi attended only the **Second** RTC (1931) — the First (1930) had no Congress representative.
practice.shortcut: First RTC = no Congress; Gandhi = Second only.

practice.q: The **Nehru Report (1928)**, India's first constitution draft, was prepared under —
practice.solution: **Motilal Nehru** chaired the committee that drafted the **Nehru Report (1928)**, demanding Dominion Status — Jinnah answered with his Fourteen Points.

practice.q: **26 January 1930** is significant because —
options: The first Independence Day was observed
practice.solution: After the **Lahore Purna Swaraj resolution (Dec 1929)**, **26 January 1930** was celebrated as Independence Day — the date later chosen for the Republic (1950).

practice.q: The **Quit India** resolution was passed on 8 August 1942 at —
practice.solution: The All India Congress Committee passed Quit India at **Gowalia Tank (August Kranti Maidan), Bombay**, with Gandhi's call: **'Do or Die'**.

practice.q: The **Rani of Jhansi Regiment** of the INA was commanded by —
practice.solution: **Captain Lakshmi Sahgal** led the INA's women's regiment under Subhas Bose's Azad Hind government (1943).

practice.q:
Who among the following were the members of the **Cabinet Mission (1946)**?
1. Lord Pethick-Lawrence
2. Stafford Cripps
3. A.V. Alexander
4. Lord Wavell
practice.solution: The **Cabinet Mission** = Pethick-Lawrence (Secretary of State), **Cripps** and **Alexander**. Wavell was the Viceroy, not a mission member.

practice.q: ***Kesari*** and ***Mahratta***, started in 1881, were edited by —
practice.solution: **Tilak** ran *Kesari* in Marathi and *Mahratta* in English — both from Pune; his 1908 *Kesari* articles led to the Mandalay sentence.

practice.q: ***Bengalee***, the newspaper associated with the Indian Association (1876), was edited by —
practice.solution: **S.N. Banerjea** used *Bengalee* to campaign for civil rights and against the 1905 partition; he founded the Indian Association in 1876.

practice.q: Which newspaper, founded in 1868, **changed its language from Bengali to English overnight** to escape the Vernacular Press Act?
practice.solution: The **Ghosh brothers' Amrita Bazar Patrika** began as a Bengali paper (Jessore, 1868); in 1878 it converted to English overnight to dodge Lytton's gag.

practice.q: The book ***Ghulamgiri*** (Slavery, 1873) was written by —
practice.solution: **Phule's *Ghulamgiri*** attacked caste slavery and the tyranny of the 'higher' castes.

practice.q: ***The Indian Struggle* (1935)**, covering 1920–34, was written by —
practice.solution: **Bose's *The Indian Struggle*** narrated the national movement of 1920–34; the book was promptly banned in British India.

practice.q:
Match:
1. *India Wins Freedom* — Maulana Abul Kalam Azad
2. *India Divided* — Rajendra Prasad
3. *Unhappy India* — Lala Lajpat Rai
Which are correct?
practice.solution: All three pairings are right: Azad's memoir, Prasad's partition critique, and Lajpat Rai's 1928 reply to *Mother India*.

practice.q: The **Vernacular Press Act (1878)** — the 'Gagging Act' — was passed by —
practice.solution: **Lytton** gagged Indian-language papers in 1878; **Ripon repealed** it in 1882.

practice.q: During the **Non-Cooperation Movement**, Gandhi's English journal was —
practice.solution: Gandhi ran ***Young India*** (English) and ***Navajivan*** (Gujarati) in the NCM years; *Harijan* began only in 1933.

practice.q: Gandhi's *Indian Opinion*, his first journal, was published from —
practice.solution: Gandhi started ***Indian Opinion*** in **1903 in South Africa**, years before his Indian journals.

practice.q: The song ***Vande Mataram*** occurs in Bankim Chandra Chatterjee's novel —
practice.solution: ***Anandamath* (1882)** contains Vande Mataram; Tagore first sang it at the **1896 Calcutta session** of the Congress.

practice.q: Rabindranath Tagore composed ***Amar Sonar Bangla*** during —
options: The Swadeshi movement against the 1905 partition
practice.solution: Written during the **1905 anti-partition agitation**, the song is now the national anthem of **Bangladesh**.

practice.q:
Consider the statements:
1. *Hind Swaraj* was written by Gandhi in 1909.
2. *Geeta Rahasya* was composed by Tilak in prison.
3. *Annihilation of Caste* was an undelivered speech of Nehru.
Which are correct?
practice.solution: *Annihilation of Caste* (1936) is **Ambedkar's** undelivered address to the Jat-Pat-Todak Mandal, not Nehru's.

practice.q: Which Governor-General is called the **'liberator of the Indian press'**?
practice.solution: **Charles Metcalfe** removed press restrictions in 1835 — press freedom stayed until the 1878 Act; Ripon later repealed that Act.
practice.shortcut: Metcalfe 1835 liberates; Lytton 1878 gags; Ripon 1882 repeals.
